title: The Mysterious Case of Iron in XMPs: Anomalous High log(Fe/O) Observed in Extremely Metal-Poor Galaxies HSCJ1631+4426 and SDSSJ0811+4730
summary: We present integral field spectroscopic observations of two local extremely metal-poor galaxies (XMPs), HSCJ1631+4426 and SDSSJ0811+4730, obtained with the Keck Cosmic Web Imager (KCWI) over the wavelength range $3545-5529$ Å at a spectral sampling of 0.5 Å, capturing bright nebular emission lines essential for determining gas-phase metallicity and chemical enrichment measurements. Using integrated spectra, we derive oxygen abundances of $\rm12+\log(O/H)=7.079\pm0.010$ and $6.926\pm0.004$, and elevated Fe/O ratios of $\rm\log(Fe/O)=-1.57\pm0.17$ and $-1.28\pm0.07$, for HSCJ1631+4426 and SDSSJ0811+4730 respectively. Each galaxy is fully contained within the $\sim$8'' field of view, with 0.15'' spaxels providing spatially resolved information. These measurements indicate unusually efficient iron enhancement at extremely low metallicity; Fe/O ratios approach or exceed solar despite oxygen abundances of only $\sim$2% solar, inconsistent with enrichment from core-collapse supernovae alone or delayed Type Ia supernovae given the young ages of the systems. Comparison with chemical evolution models suggests rare, highly energetic explosions such as bright hypernovae and/or pair-instability supernovae are likely responsible. Our results reinforce the growing evidence that XMPs can reflect the nucleosynthetic processes of early energetic stellar explosions, serving as local laboratories for chemical enrichment pathways prevalent in the early Universe.

AI.tldr: Integral field spectroscopy of two extremely metal-poor galaxies reveals elevated Fe/O ratios (~solar) despite oxygen abundances ~2% solar, suggesting enrichment from rare, highly energetic explosions like bright hypernovae or pair-instability supernovae rather than core-collapse or delayed Type Ia supernovae.
AI.motivation: To investigate chemical enrichment pathways in extremely metal-poor galaxies as local analogues for nucleosynthetic processes prevalent in the early Universe, specifically to understand the origin of enhanced iron at very low metallicity.
AI.method: Integral field spectroscopic observations using Keck Cosmic Web Imager (KCWI) over 3545–5529 Å at 0.5 Å sampling, with 0.15'' spaxels covering ~8'' field of view, on two local XMPs (HSCJ1631+4426 and SDSSJ0811+4730).
AI.result: Oxygen abundances of 12+log(O/H)=7.079±0.010 and 6.926±0.004; elevated Fe/O ratios of log(Fe/O)=−1.57±0.17 and −1.28±0.07, approaching or exceeding solar values despite ~2% solar oxygen abundance, inconsistent with core-collapse SN or delayed Ia SN enrichment given young ages.
AI.conclusion: Rare, highly energetic explosions (bright hypernovae and/or pair-instability supernovae) are likely responsible for the observed iron enhancement; XMPs serve as local laboratories for early Universe chemical enrichment pathways.

title: Enabling Cosmic Web Analysis at Gigaparsec Scales: A Multi Block Approach for DisPerSE
summary: Cosmic filaments are the longest structures in the Universe and the dominant element of the cosmic web, channelling matter onto clusters and shaping the environments in which galaxies form and evolve. Accurate reconstructions of this network across gigaparsec volumes are increasingly important for cosmology and galaxy evolution. However, the most commonly used topological filament finder, DisPerSE, faces a memory bottleneck: it requires a Delaunay tessellation of the full input point set, preventing application to large simulations. Naively splitting the volume fails, as different sub-volumes yield inconsistent tessellations and filament networks. We present a frozen-core method that overcomes this bottleneck while preserving the global topology. The volume is decomposed into overlapping blocks whose tessellations are filtered by a circumsphere criterion retaining only globally valid tetrahedra; a post-processing pipeline merges the tiled outputs through core filtering, deduplication, and boundary stitching. Validation against a monolithic reference on a $300\,h^{-1}\,\mathrm{Mpc}$ MDPL2 subvolume shows 99.6 per cent total length recovery, 100 per cent recovery of density maxima and minima, and 94.7 per cent individual filament matching (the ${\sim}$5 per cent of unmatched filaments are predominantly short, low-significance structures). We apply the method to the full $(1\,h^{-1}\,\mathrm{Gpc})^3$ MDPL2 box (92 million haloes), producing a gigaparsec-scale filament catalogue. As a first application, we measure the connectivity ($κ$) for 22,900 haloes spanning $M_{200\mathrm{c}} = 10^{12}$-$10^{15.5}\,h^{-1}\,\mathrm{M}_\odot$, finding a power-law mass-connectivity relation that extends from group to cluster scales, providing the first confirmation in an $N$-body halo catalogue that the theoretically predicted scaling holds across three decades in halo mass.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a frozen-core method to overcome the memory bottleneck of the DisPerSE filament finder, enabling gigaparsec-scale cosmic filament reconstruction. The method splits volumes into overlapping blocks, filters tessellations using a circumsphere criterion, and merges them via post-processing. It achieves 99.6% length recovery and 94.7% filament matching compared to a monolithic reference. Applied to the full (1 Gpc)^3 MDPL2 simulation, it produces a filament catalogue and confirms a power-law mass-connectivity relation across three decades in halo mass.
AI.motivation: DisPerSE, the most commonly used topological filament finder, suffers from a memory bottleneck because it requires Delaunay tessellation of the full input point set, preventing application to large simulations. Naive volume splitting fails due to inconsistent tessellations and filament networks across sub-volumes.
AI.method: A frozen-core method that decomposes the volume into overlapping blocks, tessellates each block, filters by a circumsphere criterion to retain only globally valid tetrahedra, and merges the tiled outputs via core filtering, deduplication, and boundary stitching.
AI.result: Validation on a 300 h^{-1} Mpc subvolume shows 99.6% total length recovery, 100% recovery of density maxima and minima, and 94.7% individual filament matching (unmatched filaments are primarily short, low-significance). Applied to the full (1 h^{-1} Gpc)^3 MDPL2 box with 92 million haloes, producing a gigaparsec-scale filament catalogue. Connectivity measurements for 22,900 haloes reveal a power-law mass-connectivity relation spanning three decades in halo mass.
AI.conclusion: The frozen-core method successfully overcomes DisPerSE's memory bottleneck while preserving global topology, enabling filament reconstruction at gigaparsec scales. The first confirmation of the theoretically predicted power-law mass-connectivity relation is demonstrated in an N-body halo catalogue across three decades in halo mass.

title: Fuelling the central region of galaxies with misaligned gas accretion
comment: Accepted for publication in MNRAS. 15 pages, 13 figures
summary: Recent studies have shown that the accretion of kinematically misaligned gas fuels the central reservoir of galaxies, triggering nuclear activity and star formation. In this work, we show that this specific accretion channel can only sustain main-sequence levels of star formation in galaxies with $M_* \lesssim 10^{10} {\rm M_\odot}$. Using a sample of 201 kinematically misaligned galaxies, and a comparison sample of 3689 aligned galaxies, from the Mapping Nearby Galaxies at Apache Point Observatory survey, we investigate the impact of kinematically misaligned gas on star formation across stellar mass. We characterise the global specific star formation rate, central concentration and mass of ionized gas of our samples, and derive radial profiles of specific star formation rate and ionized gas mass surface density. We find that misaligned galaxies exhibit more centrally concentrated ionized gas than their aligned counterparts, with the strongest enhancement occurring at intermediate masses ($10^{10}$-$10^{10.6} {\rm M_\odot}$), where the central ionized gas density peaks. In galaxies less massive than $10^{10} {\rm M_\odot}$, misaligned gas fuels nuclear star formation at rates typical of star-forming systems. At higher masses, however, the impact of this newly accreted gas is diluted by the larger pre-existing stellar mass in the central regions, limiting its ability to rejuvenate the star formation activity in these galaxies. Our results also show that misaligned galaxies with or without nuclear activity exhibit similar central concentrations of ionized gas, suggesting that most have a reservoir capable of fuelling their supermassive black holes over timescales longer than typical nuclear activity episodes.

AI.tldr: Using 201 misaligned and 3689 aligned galaxies from MaNGA, the authors find that kinematically misaligned gas accretion fuels main-sequence star formation only in galaxies with M* ≲ 10¹⁰ M☉. The impact diminishes at higher masses due to dilution by pre-existing stellar mass. Misaligned galaxies show centrally concentrated ionized gas, with the strongest enhancement at intermediate masses (10¹⁰–10¹⁰.⁶ M☉). Most misaligned galaxies, regardless of nuclear activity, possess sufficient central gas reservoirs to sustain black hole fueling over long timescales.
AI.motivation: To understand how kinematically misaligned gas accretion influences star formation and nuclear activity across the stellar mass range, and to determine the mass regime where this accretion channel can sustain star formation at main-sequence levels.
AI.method: Used a sample of 201 kinematically misaligned galaxies and 3689 aligned galaxies from the MaNGA survey. Measured global specific star formation rate (sSFR), central concentration and mass of ionized gas, and derived radial profiles of sSFR and ionized gas mass surface density.
AI.result: Misaligned galaxies have more centrally concentrated ionized gas than aligned ones, with strongest enhancement at 10¹⁰–10¹⁰.⁶ M☉. For M* ≲ 10¹⁰ M☉, misaligned gas fuels nuclear star formation at main-sequence levels. At higher masses, the accreted gas is diluted by pre-existing stellar mass. Misaligned galaxies with and without nuclear activity show similar central ionized gas concentrations.
AI.conclusion: Kinematically misaligned gas accretion can sustain main-sequence star formation only in low-mass galaxies (M* ≲ 10¹⁰ M☉). In more massive galaxies, the effect is diluted. Most misaligned galaxies have central gas reservoirs capable of sustaining supermassive black hole fueling over timescales longer than typical nuclear activity episodes.

title: Discrepancies between Chandrasekhar's theory of relaxation and $N$-body simulations
comment: 13 pages, 12 figures, 3 tables, submitted to A&A
summary: Globular clusters are systems which are known to be particularly well described by two-body relaxation. In recent decades many studies have shown that Chandrasekhar's orbit-averaged theory is able to reproduce many features of numerical simulations. However, it has been claimed that differences between the theory and simulation remain, such as an amplitude mismatch of the rate of change of the distribution function. In this paper we compare the theoretical predictions of Chandrasekhar's theory for anisotropic clusters to precise $N$-body data. We show that more careful $N$-body measurements are able to reduce the claimed mismatch. Nevertheless, we observe a dependency of the remaining mismatch on both position and anisotropy. While the dependence on anisotropy may be understood qualitatively on theoretical grounds, the radial dependence implies that spatial inhomogeneities, and therefore collective effects, may become unavoidable to resolve the residual mismatch between theory and simulations.

AI.tldr: This paper revisits Chandrasekhar's orbit-averaged theory for globular clusters, showing that careful N-body measurements reduce the previously claimed mismatch, but residual discrepancies depending on position and anisotropy remain, suggesting spatial inhomogeneities and collective effects may be needed to fully resolve them.
AI.motivation: To resolve claimed discrepancies between Chandrasekhar's orbit-averaged theory and N-body simulations for anisotropic globular clusters, particularly an amplitude mismatch in the rate of change of the distribution function.
AI.method: Comparison of theoretical predictions from Chandrasekhar's orbit-averaged theory to precise N-body simulations, with careful measurement techniques to reduce systematic errors.
AI.result: More careful N-body measurements reduce the claimed mismatch, but a residual mismatch persists that depends on both radial position and anisotropy.
AI.conclusion: The radial dependence of the residual mismatch suggests that spatial inhomogeneities and collective effects may be necessary to fully reconcile theory with simulations.

title: The COLIBRE-SKIRT pipeline: Calibration-free dust radiative transfer postprocessing for cosmological simulations
comment: Main text 23 pages and 8 figures. Submitted to A&A
summary: Context. Three-dimensional dust radiative transfer provides a powerful framework to connect cosmological galaxy simulations to multiwavelength observations. Until recently, in large-volume simulations, the formation of a cold ISM phase was prevented and dust was not evolved self-consistently. This required calibration of dust-to-metal ratios and extra subgrid dust attenuation in birth clouds, thereby reducing the predictive power. Aims. We present the COLIBRE-SKIRT pipeline, a calibration-free dust radiative transfer framework for the novel COLIBRE suite of large-volume cosmological simulations, which include a live dust model and directly simulate the multiphase ISM. Our primary aim is to establish a reference pipeline for generating multiwavelength mock observables from these simulations. As a first application, we produce far-ultraviolet (FUV) to far-infrared (FIR) spatially integrated spectra and assess them by comparison with the observed low-redshift cosmic spectral energy distribution (CSED). Methods. We apply the SKIRT dust radiative transfer code to the COLIBRE simulations. Dust masses and species fractions are taken directly from the simulation, and no birth cloud model is added in postprocessing. We introduce a "split & scale" approach that maps the simulated two-size, multi-species dust distribution onto continuous grain size distributions without introducing free parameters. Results. We find that, for the first time, a large-volume cosmological simulation directly reproduces the local Universe CSED without calibrating the postprocessing routine a priori. Residual tensions in the mid-infrared (~0.2 dex) point towards insufficient heating of the hottest dust components and uncertainties in the modelling of the PAH-emission carriers. This framework can be readily applied at low and high redshift to create synthetic spectra and images from the FUV to the FIR.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the COLIBRE-SKIRT pipeline, a calibration-free dust radiative transfer framework for large-volume cosmological simulations. It successfully reproduces the observed low-redshift cosmic spectral energy distribution (CSED) from FUV to FIR without prior calibration, using a novel "split & scale" method to map simulated dust distributions onto continuous grain size distributions.
AI.motivation: Previous large-volume cosmological simulations required calibration of dust-to-metal ratios and subgrid dust attenuation in birth clouds, reducing predictive power. The goal is to establish a calibration-free pipeline that can generate multiwavelength mock observables from simulations that include a live dust model and directly simulate the multiphase ISM.
AI.method: The SKIRT dust radiative transfer code is applied to COLIBRE simulations. Dust masses and species fractions are taken directly from simulation without adding a birth cloud model in postprocessing. A "split & scale" approach is introduced to map the simulated two-size, multi-species dust distribution onto continuous grain size distributions without introducing free parameters.
AI.result: For the first time, a large-volume cosmological simulation directly reproduces the local Universe CSED without calibrating the postprocessing routine a priori. Residual tensions in the mid-infrared (~0.2 dex) indicate insufficient heating of the hottest dust components and uncertainties in PAH-emission carrier modelling.
AI.conclusion: The COLIBRE-SKIRT pipeline is a calibration-free framework that can be readily applied at low and high redshift to create synthetic spectra and images from the FUV to the FIR, representing a significant step forward in connecting cosmological galaxy simulations to multiwavelength observations.

title: The Goldilocks Molecule: H$_{2}$ Emission Lines Can Identify Elusive Dwarf AGN
summary: We propose using H$_{2}$ emission lines as a novel diagnostic to identify dwarf AGN by running photoionization models incorporating active intermediate-mass black holes and using an observed WISE dwarf AGN as a template. Though many dwarf AGN would be incorrectly classified as star-forming if the H$_{2}$~2.12~$μ$m/Br$γ$ ratio is used, ratios between H$_{2}$ emission lines can reveal active IMBHs in cases where log $n_{\text{H}} \gtrsim 4.0$. This includes the case where $M_{\text{BH}} = 10^3~M_{\odot}$, even though the optical strong lines and NIR coronal lines would likely go undetected. We conclude that H$_{2}$ emission lines show promise in detecting the most elusive IMBHs.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes using H₂ emission lines as a new diagnostic to detect dwarf AGN with intermediate-mass black holes (IMBHs), particularly effective when hydrogen density log n_H ≥ 4.0, even when optical and NIR coronal lines are undetectable.
AI.motivation: Current methods fail to detect elusive intermediate-mass black holes (IMBHs) in dwarf galaxies because optical strong lines and NIR coronal lines often go undetected, leaving many dwarf AGN misclassified as star-forming.
AI.method: Running photoionization models incorporating active intermediate-mass black holes and using an observed WISE dwarf AGN as a template; analyzing ratios between H₂ emission lines (e.g., H₂ 2.12 μm/Brγ) under varying hydrogen density and black hole mass conditions.
AI.result: H₂ emission line ratios can reveal active IMBHs when log n_H ≳ 4.0, including cases with M_BH = 10³ M⊙, where optical and NIR coronal lines remain undetected; however, the H₂ 2.12 μm/Brγ ratio alone would misclassify many dwarf AGN as star-forming.
AI.conclusion: H₂ emission lines are a promising diagnostic for detecting the most elusive IMBHs that evade traditional optical and NIR line diagnostics.

title: Isomer-specific excitation of formic acid in collisions with helium atoms
summary: An accurate estimation of the molecular abundances of isomers in the interstellar medium (ISM) is necessary to unravel the underlying chemistry and physics. After the recent detections of both isomers of formic acid ($cis-$ and $trans-$HCOOH) in dense dark cold clouds, their accurate molecular line modeling became of interest. The conditions of these environments do not necessarily follow the local thermodynamic equilibrium, thus taking into account the competition between the radiative and collisional processes is required. This involves the knowledge of the rotational excitation data for collisions with the most abundant interstellar species \textemdash He and H$_2$. In this paper, the first potential energy surfaces (PES) for the interaction of the two rotamers of formic acid with He atoms are computed using the explicitly correlated coupled-cluster theory [CCSD(T)-F12]. The obtained PESs demonstrate qualitative similarities and high anisotropy. The global minima are found with $V=-53.0$ cm$^{-1}$ and $V=-46.0$ cm$^{-1}$ for $cis-$HCOOH and $trans-$HCOOH respectively. Collisional excitation cross sections calculated for total energies up to 100 cm$^{-1}$ demonstrate similar propensity rules for both isomers. Quantitative differences of the cross sections associated with the two rotamers are also discussed.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the first potential energy surfaces (PES) for collisions between both isomers of formic acid (cis- and trans-HCOOH) and He atoms, computed using CCSD(T)-F12 theory. The PESs show qualitative similarities with global minima at -53.0 cm⁻¹ (cis) and -46.0 cm⁻¹ (trans). Collisional excitation cross sections up to 100 cm⁻¹ reveal similar propensity rules but quantitative differences between the two rotamers.
AI.motivation: Accurate modeling of molecular line emissions in dense dark cold clouds requires non-LTE treatment, which depends on collisional excitation data with He and H₂. After recent detections of both formic acid isomers in the ISM, such data became necessary for understanding the underlying interstellar chemistry.
AI.method: The authors compute the first potential energy surfaces for cis- and trans-HCOOH interacting with He using the explicitly correlated coupled-cluster theory CCSD(T)-F12, then calculate collisional excitation cross sections for total energies up to 100 cm⁻¹.
AI.result: Both PESs show qualitative similarities and high anisotropy. Global minima: cis-HCOOH at -53.0 cm⁻¹, trans-HCOOH at -46.0 cm⁻¹. Cross sections exhibit similar propensity rules for both isomers with quantitative differences between the rotamers.
AI.conclusion: The computed PES and collisional data enable accurate non-LTE modeling of formic acid isomers in interstellar environments, with quantitative differences between rotamers important for distinguishing them observationally.

title: The World Cup in space: Finding ionised buckyballs in the ISM with CARMENES
comment: To appear in Highlights of Spanish Astrophysics XIII, Proceedings of the XVII Scientific Meeting of the Spanish Astronomical Society held on 13-17 July 2026, in Tarragona, Spain
summary: Over a century after the discovery of the first diffuse interstellar bands (DIBs) in absorption in stellar spectra (Heger et al 1922), their origin is still mostly unknown. The exception are four DIBs (out of 600+ known) in the 9300-9700 Angstrom region, for which a possible ascription to C_60^+ (ionised buckminsterfullerene, shaped liked a football, hence buckyballs) has been made. However, those DIBs are located in a spectral region heavily contaminated by telluric H_2O absorption, hampering their detection and study from the ground. I present the results of a study with the CARMENES spectrograph that uses a novel technique with multi-epoch spectroscopy at different times of the year to shift the relative position of the DIBs and the surrounding telluric lines, hence facilitating the analysis of the DIBs. The technique has been applied to 41 sightlines of diverse extinctions and environments, with positive detections in all of them. Our results are consistent with three of those DIBs having C_60^+ as the carrier.

AI.tldr: This paper uses a novel multi-epoch spectroscopic technique with CARMENES to observe C60+ diffuse interstellar bands (DIBs) in the telluric-contaminated 9300-9700 Å region across 41 sightlines, confirming three DIBs as likely originating from ionized buckminsterfullerene.
AI.motivation: Most DIBs (600+) discovered over a century remain unidentified; four DIBs possibly attributed to C60+ lie in a spectral region heavily contaminated by telluric H2O absorption, making ground-based detection and study difficult.
AI.method: Multi-epoch spectroscopy with the CARMENES spectrograph, using observations at different times of the year to shift relative positions of DIBs and telluric lines, applied to 41 sightlines across diverse extinction environments.
AI.result: Positive detections of C60+ DIBs in all 41 sightlines; consistent with three of those DIBs having C60+ as the carrier.
AI.conclusion: The novel multi-epoch technique successfully mitigates telluric contamination, and the results support C60+ as the carrier for three DIBs in the 9300-9700 Å region.

title: Berkeley 32: A Metal-poor and Dynamically Evolved Open Cluster with Evidence of Radial Migration
comment: 27 pages, including 15 figures and 4 tables, accepted for publication in the The Astronomical Journal (AJ)
summary: We present a comprehensive chemo-dynamical analysis of the old, metal-poor open cluster Berkeley 32 based on Gaia DR3 astrometry and Gaia-ESO Survey DR5.1 spectroscopy. Cluster membership is determined using a Gaussian Mixture Model applied to proper-motion components and trigonometric parallaxes. Isochrone fitting yields an age of 4.9 +/- 0.5 Gyr, a heliocentric distance of 3325 pc, and an extinction of A_V = 0.38 +/- 0.12 mag. Spectroscopic member stars exhibit a mean metallicity of [Fe/H] = -0.39 +/- 0.02 dex, near-solar alpha-element abundances, and a weighted mean radial velocity of V_rad = 106.26 +/- 0.03 km s^-1. The [Y/Mg] chemical clock yields an age of 4.73 +/- 2.39 Gyr, consistent with the isochrone estimate. Orbital integration indicates a moderately eccentric orbit (e = 0.268 +/- 0.004) with a guiding radius of R_g = 8.82 kpc. The inferred chemical birth radius, R_b = 9.82 kpc, together with DeltaR ~ -1 kpc, suggests moderate inward radial migration, while the offsets among R_b, R_g, and R_GC are consistent with both churning and blurring processes. A photometric analysis identifies a binary fraction of f_b = 0.449 +/- 0.017 for systems with mass ratios q >= 0.5, implying a substantial unresolved binary population. Radial cumulative distribution functions further reveal significant mass segregation, with evolved stars more centrally concentrated than main-sequence stars. These results indicate that Berkeley 32 is a dynamically evolved old-disk cluster whose present-day structure and orbit preserve signatures of both internal dynamical evolution and radial migration within the Galactic disk.

AI.tldr: Berkeley 32 is a 4.9 Gyr old, metal-poor ([Fe/H] = -0.39 dex) open cluster located 3325 pc away, with near-solar alpha abundances, moderate eccentricity (e=0.268), and signs of inward radial migration (~1 kpc). It has a high binary fraction (44.9%) and shows mass segregation, indicating significant internal dynamical evolution.
AI.motivation: To characterize the chemo-dynamical properties of the old, metal-poor open cluster Berkeley 32, and to investigate its internal dynamical evolution and radial migration history within the Galactic disk.
AI.method: Gaia DR3 astrometry + Gaia-ESO DR5.1 spectroscopy; Gaussian Mixture Model for membership; isochrone fitting; [Y/Mg] chemical clock; orbital integration; photometric binary analysis; radial cumulative distribution functions for mass segregation.
AI.result: Age 4.9±0.5 Gyr; distance 3325 pc; A_V=0.38±0.12; [Fe/H]=-0.39±0.02; near-solar [α/Fe]; V_rad=106.26±0.03 km/s; [Y/Mg] age 4.73±2.39 Gyr; e=0.268±0.004; R_g=8.82 kpc; R_b=9.82 kpc; ΔR~ -1 kpc; binary fraction 0.449±0.017 (q≥0.5); mass segregation present.
AI.conclusion: Berkeley 32 is a dynamically evolved old-disk cluster, with its present-day structure and orbit preserving signatures of both internal dynamical evolution and radial migration within the Galactic disk.

title: Cluster characteristics of Galactic open clusters
summary: Star clusters are perfectly suited for studying the formation, evolution, and dynamics of stars and their host galaxies. For this, we need to estimate total masses, radii and shapes of star clusters. These parameters strongly influence their fates in the host galaxies. However, there is no agreement about these characteristics in the literature. The published values widely disagree. We estimated total masses and cluster radii using a very conservative approach: calculating member masses and summing them. Furthermore, we investigated the three-dimensional characteristics of open clusters and their limitations. We used a commonly used grid of evolutionary tracks for different photometric sources, including 2MASS, Gaia, and Pan-STARRS. The interpolation method was tested using synthetic clusters built with ASteCA. To estimate three-dimensional shapes, we used the distribution of the well-known Galactic coordinates and inverse parallaxes. We estimated the total masses and radii of about 7000 open clusters and observed traces of tidal tails. Individual values can be used in future $Gaia$ data releases to obtain even more precise values. The current DR3 allows the study of only three-dimensional shapes up to 500 pc. Beyond this distance, we find a significant needle-like shape due to uncertainties in observed parallaxes.

AI.tldr: Analyzed ~7000 open clusters using conservative member mass summation and 3D shape estimation from Gaia/2MASS/Pan-STARRS data, finding tidal tail traces and limiting reliable 3D shape measurements to within 500 pc due to parallax uncertainties.
AI.motivation: Star cluster parameters (mass, radius, shape) strongly influence their evolution and fate in host galaxies, yet published values widely disagree, necessitating a consistent, conservative estimation approach.
AI.method: Conservative mass estimation by summing individual member masses; 3D shape analysis using Galactic coordinates and inverse parallaxes; interpolation tested with ASteCA synthetic clusters; multi-survey photometry (2MASS, Gaia, Pan-STARRS) with evolutionary track grids.
AI.result: Estimated total masses and radii for ~7000 open clusters; detected tidal tail features; found reliable 3D shape characterization limited to <500 pc due to significant needle-like artifacts from parallax uncertainties beyond that distance.
AI.conclusion: Conservative member-summation approach provides consistent cluster parameters; Gaia DR3 enables 3D shape study only within 500 pc; future data releases can improve precision; individual values are provided for further use.

title: The Open Cluster Chemical Abundances and Mapping Survey: IX. Measuring the Effects of Stellar Diffusion in the Open Clusters NGC 752 and Ruprecht 147 using APOGEE
comment: Accepted for publication in the ApJ
summary: A growing understanding of stellar processes that alter surface chemical abundances over time has opened new avenues for using these changes as probes of stellar properties. On the main sequence and near the turnoff, stellar surface abundances are affected by gravitational settling and radiative acceleration, collectively known as atomic diffusion. In this work, we use SDSS/APOGEE DR17/DR19 data to investigate atomic diffusion in the open clusters NGC~752 and Ruprecht~147, thereby constraining how these signatures vary with age. From the analysis of Fe, C, N, Na, Mg, Al, Si, S, K, Ca, Ti, V, Cr, Mn, Co, and Ni, we find significant abundance differences between stars near the turnoff and the cooler main-sequence, where warmer stars are depleted relative to the cooler main-sequence stars at the $\geq1σ$ level for all elements available in the analysis. These abundance differences are consistent with the signatures expected from atomic diffusion and are further supported by comparisons with stellar models that include diffusion. By fitting the observed $T_{\rm eff}$--[Fe/H] patterns with MIST isochrones, we obtain best-fit ages of 1.0~Gyr for NGC~752 and 2.5--3.2~Gyr for Ruprecht~147. Carbon is a key diagnostic, as it shows both atomic diffusion and extra-mixing signatures associated with first-dredge-up. For NGC~752, the coolest stars in our sample, which provide the best proxy for the initial cluster composition, yield [Fe/H]$_{\rm CS} = 0.01~\pm~0.02(\pm~0.05)$ dex. For Ruprecht~147, we obtain [Fe/H]$_{\rm CS} = 0.17~\pm~0.00(\pm~0.05)$ dex. Our findings further constrain atomic diffusion models, suggesting that atomic diffusion affects age estimates of stars near the main-sequence turnoff.

AI.tldr: This study investigates atomic diffusion (gravitational settling and radiative acceleration) in open clusters NGC 752 and Ruprecht 147 using SDSS/APOGEE DR17/DR19 data. Significant abundance differences between turnoff and cooler main-sequence stars are found across 16 elements, consistent with diffusion models. Best-fit ages are 1.0 Gyr (NGC 752) and 2.5–3.2 Gyr (Ruprecht 147), with cluster metallicities [Fe/H]=0.01±0.02 and 0.17±0.00 dex respectively. Carbon shows both diffusion and first-dredge-up mixing signatures. Results demonstrate that atomic diffusion affects age estimates of stars near the main-sequence turnoff.
AI.motivation: To constrain how atomic diffusion signatures (gravitational settling and radiative acceleration) vary with stellar age by analyzing open clusters of different ages, and to understand how these processes affect stellar abundance measurements and age estimates.
AI.method: Analyzed 16 elemental abundances (Fe, C, N, Na, Mg, Al, Si, S, K, Ca, Ti, V, Cr, Mn, Co, Ni) from SDSS/APOGEE DR17/DR19 data for open clusters NGC 752 and Ruprecht 147. Compared observed Teff–[Fe/H] patterns with MIST isochrones and diffusion-inclusive stellar models to constrain ages and diffusion signatures.
AI.result: Significant abundance differences (≥1σ) found between turnoff and cooler main-sequence stars across all 16 elements, with warmer stars depleted relative to cooler stars. Best-fit ages: 1.0 Gyr (NGC 752) and 2.5–3.2 Gyr (Ruprecht 147). Cluster metallicities: [Fe/H]=0.01±0.02 (NGC 752) and 0.17±0.00 (Ruprecht 147). Carbon exhibits both diffusion and extra-mixing (first-dredge-up) signatures.
AI.conclusion: Atomic diffusion significantly affects age estimates of stars near the main-sequence turnoff. The observed abundance patterns are consistent with diffusion models, and the results provide observational constraints for improving atomic diffusion models in stellar evolution.

title: Runaway OB stars within 1 kpc of the Sun
summary: Runaway stars are high-velocity stars ejected from their birth environments that can provide insights into the kinematic history of the stellar cluster they were ejected from. We derived runaway star probabilities for 40 O-type stars and $24,487$ B-type stars taken from a recently published volume-complete sample of OB stars within 1 kpc of the Sun. We fit a Galactic rotation model to the observed proper motions of these stars and identify runaway stars using both a fixed 2D peculiar velocity threshold of $23\,km\,s^{-1}$ and by comparing individual peculiar velocities to the dispersion of the whole sample. We find runaway fractions of $17.5^{+0.1}_{-2.5}\%$ for O-type stars and $6.9\pm0.1\%$ for B-type stars; both using the fixed velocity threshold method. These values are consistent with previous studies, but with differences that are largely attributable to the underlying samples of OB stars used in various studies to identify runaway stars and to variations in the methods used to select them.

AI.tldr: This study analyzes runaway stars among 40 O-type and 24,487 B-type stars within 1 kpc of the Sun, finding runaway fractions of 17.5% for O-type and 6.9% for B-type stars using a fixed 2D peculiar velocity threshold of 23 km/s and Galactic rotation modeling.
AI.motivation: Runaway stars provide insights into the kinematic history of their birth stellar clusters, and understanding their fractions and properties helps constrain ejection mechanisms and cluster dynamics.
AI.method: A Galactic rotation model was fit to observed proper motions of a volume-complete sample of OB stars within 1 kpc. Runaway stars were identified using a fixed 2D peculiar velocity threshold of 23 km/s and by comparing individual peculiar velocities to the sample dispersion.
AI.result: Runaway fractions: 17.5% for O-type stars and 6.9% for B-type stars (fixed threshold method). Results are consistent with previous studies, with differences attributed to sample selection and methodology variations.
AI.conclusion: The derived runaway fractions are broadly consistent with prior work, but sample composition and identification methods significantly affect the results.

title: Stellar Multiplicity in Open Clusters: Investigating Binary Fractions and Their Relationship with Cluster Properties
summary: Stellar multiplicity is key in dynamical evolution of open clusters (OCs) and processes of stellar formation and evolution. Since most stars form in multiple systems, investigating how environmental properties affect their occurrence is crucial. We aim to investigate how binary fraction and mass ratios change across different OC environments. Using a sample of 773 OCs, we identified binary systems and estimated binary fractions, obtaining values in the ranges 0.10-0.85 overall and 0.06-0.79 for high mass-ratio systems. No strong dependence on age or evolutionary stage is found, while an anticorrelation between metallicity and the binary fraction is identified. However, young and old clusters exhibit distinct mass-ratio distributions. We also find that the probability of a star being the primary component increases with stellar mass. In contrast, the probability of a star belonging to a binary system increases with mass for masses below 1 solar mass, and remains between 60% and 70% for high masses. Binary systems are preferentially located in the inner regions of clusters compared to single stars, and the mean mass ratio decreases with increasing distance from the cluster center. These results suggest that the binary fraction appears to be set at early times and remains largely unaffected by cluster dynamical evolution. The concentration of binaries in the inner regions of clusters likely reduces their susceptibility to dynamical escape.

AI.tldr: Using 773 open clusters, this study finds binary fractions of 0.10-0.85 (0.06-0.79 for high mass-ratio systems), with no strong age dependence but an anticorrelation with metallicity. Binary probability increases with mass below 1 M☉ (60-70% at high masses), and binaries concentrate in cluster inner regions where mean mass ratios are higher.
AI.motivation: To understand how environmental properties of open clusters affect binary fraction and mass ratios, given that most stars form in multiple systems and stellar multiplicity influences cluster dynamics and stellar evolution.
AI.method: Analyzed a sample of 773 open clusters, identified binary systems, estimated binary fractions and mass-ratio distributions, and examined correlations with cluster age, metallicity, stellar mass, and radial position.
AI.result: Binary fractions range 0.10-0.85 overall; no strong age dependence; anticorrelation with metallicity; distinct mass-ratio distributions between young and old clusters; probability of being primary increases with mass; binary probability rises with mass below 1 M☉ then plateaus at 60-70%; binaries concentrated in inner regions where mass ratios are higher.
AI.conclusion: Binary fraction is set at early times and largely unaffected by dynamical evolution; binary concentration in cluster cores reduces their susceptibility to dynamical escape.

title: The non-LTE abundances of magnesium and yttrium and asteroseismic ages for the chemical clock calibration
summary: Building on our previous study, which demonstrated the importance of accounting for departures from local thermodynamic equilibrium (LTE) in elemental-abundance determinations and of using asteroseismic ages, we investigate spatial variations in the empirical [Y/Mg]-age relation across the Galactic disc using a substantially larger stellar sample. We analysed high-resolution stellar spectra and determined Mg and Y abundances through spectral synthesis of multiple spectral features, rigorously accounting for non-LTE (NLTE) effects. We derived asteroseismic ages for stars exhibiting solar-type oscillations and used cross-checked isochrone-based methods for the remaining stars. We determined atmospheric parameters and Mg and Y abundances for 528 Galactic field stars, together with asteroseismic ages for 307 stars and isochronal ages for 221 stars. We also identified two new triple-lined and nine double-lined spectroscopic systems. Combining the present sample with that of our previous study yielded a total of 736 stars, which we used to examine the [Y/Mg]-age relation across the Galactic disc. The relation shows systematic spatial variations that likely reflect differences in star-formation and chemical-enrichment histories. In general, [Y/Mg] tends to increase with metallicity over the investigated age range. At supersolar metallicity, however, this trend may weaken, and the [Y/Mg]-age relations become flatter than those of solar-metallicity stars, which show lower [Y/Mg] values at young ages and higher values at old ages.

AI.tldr: This study uses 736 stars (528 new + 208 from previous work) with NLTE-corrected Mg/Y abundances and asteroseismic/isochronal ages to map the [Y/Mg]-age relation across the Galactic disc, finding systematic spatial variations tied to star-formation and chemical-enrichment histories, with metallicity-dependent behavior.
AI.motivation: To investigate spatial variations in the empirical [Y/Mg]-age relation across the Galactic disc using a larger stellar sample, building on prior work showing the necessity of accounting for NLTE effects and using asteroseismic ages for abundance determinations.
AI.method: High-resolution stellar spectra analyzed via spectral synthesis for Mg and Y abundances with rigorous NLTE corrections; asteroseismic ages derived for solar-type oscillators (307 stars) and isochrone-based ages for others (221 stars); combined with previous sample to total 736 stars; spectroscopic binaries identified (2 triple-lined, 9 double-lined).
AI.result: The [Y/Mg]-age relation shows systematic spatial variations across the disc, reflecting differences in star-formation and chemical-enrichment histories. [Y/Mg] generally increases with metallicity; at supersolar metallicity the trend weakens and the relation flattens, while solar-metallicity stars show lower [Y/Mg] at young ages and higher at old ages.
AI.conclusion: Accounting for NLTE effects and using precise ages is critical for reliable abundance-age relations; the [Y/Mg]-age relation is not universal across the Galactic disc but varies with location and metallicity, implying distinct chemical evolution histories.
